cells.tense: What your heart already knows has settled into a still place, and the ending is here with the pen.
cells.act: read the hardest page of it twice, slowly, before you stop
cells.ask: Take the hardest page of what's over between you and someone, and read it twice, slowly, all the way down. Once more through, then stop there.
cells.core:
Some things you've carried with people have already ended, quietly, and your heart knows it. What's harder is the page you keep skipping — the one about a bond or a way of being together that's finished but that you haven't let yourself finish reading. You're resting in the stillness, which is real, and you're resting there partly so you don't have to turn that page. The completion is the point, not a failure of the peace.

Reading that hard page a second time, slowly, all the way down, is the work. Depth finishes a thing rather than leaving it half-open. The stillness you have now isn't broken by reading it — the stillness after a page is read runs deeper than the stillness before, because nothing is still waiting. You come out of the reading lighter than the pen.
cells.sheetLine: Read the page that's over before you turn past it.
cells.place: at the edge of what's ending

cells.tense: You are standing in the after of a connection that hasn't ended, guarding against a loss still out of sight.
cells.act: count what the ending gave you
cells.ask: Pick one connection between you and someone that's already over, and count what it gave you — the real yield, not the loss. Once, before anything else.
cells.core:
A connection has been stable, and you've already moved into its after, bracing for a loss that hasn't happened. The stillness isn't peace; it's pulling out in front of someone who is still beside you, defending a bond nobody is attacking. From their side, the distance is what they feel, and it's steady.

What the ending actually gave you is what's waiting to be gathered, not what's waiting to be guarded. Count the yield of one finished thing — what it grew in you and between you. Counting isn't grief and isn't denial; it's what the change already produced. Do that before you turn it into a story about what you're about to lose. The balance you're reaching for is felt recognition: you and the other person, both real, neither dissolved into the other.
cells.sheetLine: Nobody is taking the bond away. Stop guarding it.
cells.place: at the edge of what's ending

cells.tense: The ending already happened, and you are still standing at a door that's behind you.
cells.act: gather the scattered thoughts into one line
cells.ask: Gather the pieces you keep going back and forth on into one sentence: this ended. Say it once, plainly, and stop there.
cells.core: Something between you and people you love has ended, and you're still keeping the old words said. The ending isn't the hard part — the hard part is arriving late to your own life, with the pieces of what happened still scattered and nothing to stand on. Your thinking is the way in: gather those pieces into one line, a sentence that says plainly what ended. Not why, not who was right — just what's over. When the thought finds its line, the feeling can land in the present, where the ending actually is. This isn't pushing feeling somewhere it isn't; it's letting the mind do what the mind is good at so the rest of you can catch up. One sentence, said once, is where you meet yourself.
cells.sheetLine: The door's behind you. Stand where the ending is.
cells.place: at the edge of what's ending

cells.tense: You are already letting something end by not renewing it, and the one doing the letting is you, unsigned.
cells.act: let the mind find its own limit in the thing
cells.ask: You're letting something end by not renewing it. Follow what you're doing all the way to where your thinking runs out on it. No conclusions — just follow it there.
cells.core:
A way of being close to someone — a rhythm, a bond you've stopped feeding — is already ending, gently, by your own not renewing it. The peace in you is real, and it's partly what the ending made. But the ending is authored, and the author hasn't signed it, so it lives in you as a thinning instead of a completion.

Follow it down to where your understanding of it runs out — the point past which you can't think your way further. Not a story about why, just the edge of what you can hold. Reaching that limit doesn't undo the ending; it gives the ending a self. The peace that comes after you sign it holds steadier than the peace that comes after you don't.
cells.sheetLine: The ending is already happening by your hand. Say so to yourself.
cells.place: at the edge of what's ending

A reader could reasonably say the Too Much core names a specific habit (ending before anyone's eaten) that may not fit. The sentence that serves me more than the person is the sheetLine for Balanced — 'let what's over be over' was a slogan doing no work; I replaced it with the quieter line.
